newsitem.title: CYPRUS: US envoy in Cyprus says military agreement reached.
newsitem.headline: US envoy in Cyprus says military agreement reached.

text.p: A U.S. envoy on a peace mission to Cyprus said on Monday said the two sides on the militarily divided island had agreed steps to reduce tension along a ceasefire line separating them.

"Both sides today gave their support to very quick and immediate implementation of that pack of proposals," U.S. State Department official Carey Cavanaugh told journalists before leaving the island for Athens.

Cavanaugh, on the island to defuse a row which broke out after Cyprus's decision to purchase Russian anti-aircraft missiles and Turkish threats of a military strike to stop their deployment, said the proposals would help reduce tension on the divided island.

The United Nations-backed proposals relate to unloading of live ammunition by soldiers on either side of the 180 km (110 mile) ceasefire line which has split Cyprus's Greek and Turkish Cypriot communities for two decades, and unmanning sentry posts. It also imposes a code of conduct for the soldiers to follow.
"These measures reduce the likelihood of incidents along the ceasefire line," Cavanaugh said.
Earlier, Cavanaugh said there was no crisis in Cyprus because its government had assured him it would not bring in any part the missile system for at least 16 months.
"I believe that should effectively defuse this as a crisis issue for Cyprus," he said after an hour-long meeting with Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides on Monday morning.

Turkey -- which has occupied the northern third of the island since 1974 -- threatened military action several times last week to stop deployment of the S-300 system which the Cypriot government said it would acquire from Russia.
The Turkish Cypriot administration in the north of the island and Turkey have said they will not allow the deployment of the missiles, which the Cypriot government says are purely defensive.
"We will do all that is necessary in order to avert the arrival of the missiles," Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash said after meeting Cavanaugh on Monday afternoon.
"After 16 months, if they arrive, they create the crisis again. Turkey has made it absolutely clear that it will not allow the missiles to come," he said.
Cavanaugh, whose government has criticised Cyprus's decision to purchase the system, reiterated that any Turkish response would be unacceptable and unjustified.
He said that any crisis has been "significantly postponed".
"It has moved so far into the future that there should be adequate time to work to address the problem," he said.
Turkey's armed forces chief, General Ismail Hakki Karadayi, arrived in northern Cyprus on Monday saying Greek Cypriot plans were the "culmination of provocation and over-militarisation".

"Let no one forget what the real purpose is," he told reporters. "You cannot show a weapon that has a range of 150 to 160 km (93 to 100 miles) as a defensive system. This is not acceptable and it cannot be taken lightly," Karadayi said.

Denktash's administration, declared a breakaway Turkish Cypriot state in 1983 recognised only by Ankara, has also said it will move people into Varosha, a now empty tourist resort once mainly owned by Greek Cypriots but now in Turkish held territory.
Cyprus has been divided since 1974 when Turkey invaded the north of the island after a coup in Nicosia engineered by the military junta then ruling Greece.
Turkey has around 30,000 troops in the north of Cyprus as opposed to 11,500 men of the Greek Cypriot national guard in the south.
